title: Schema-driven offload and client mediator PRD (wip)
body:
Purpose
This doc sketches a pragmatic PRD for an SDK-side mediator and server-driven schema offload that together reduce client complexity for streaming tool-calls and structured responses. It is explicitly an experiment-driven approach: small changes to the runtime and a lightweight SDK shim that lets product teams migrate incrementally.

Problem space
- Teams building with Hosted API struggle to: manage partial streaming frames for structured outputs, coordinate tool calls (and retries/fallbacks) in unstable networks, and keep client SDK ergonomics simple across platforms (web, mobile, server).
- Two recurring sources of bugs and engineering costs: ad-hoc client-side reassembly of partial JSON/frames and bespoke tool-call orchestration logic (retries, idempotency, credential exchange).

Goals (measurable)
- Reduce client-side integration surface by providing a canonical SDK mediator that handles incremental frames, structured schema validation, and tool-call lifecycle. Metric: reduce client code lines for integration by 50% for reference integrations.
- Improve structured-output correctness under network instability: target 99.5% of streamed JSON payloads validate against schema on first pass for our top-10 customers.
- Provide deterministic fallback behavior for tool call failures, reducing customer-observed tool-related errors by 30% in first 3 months.

Non-goals
- This PRD does not introduce new low-level wire protocols; it reuses the existing event/stream framing with a small optional metadata envelope.
- We are not adding new authentication types for tools (KMS/HSM work is separate).

High-level approach
1) Server: schema-offload endpoint and schema-aware partial frames. When a model invocation is created with a structured output contract (schema id), the runtime will attach a schema id and optional canonical failure modes to the stream. The schema itself lives in the project namespace and can be versioned.
2) SDK mediator: an opt-in lightweight component for official SDKs that: a) buffers and reassembles partial frames, b) validates against schema chunks as they arrive (incremental validation where possible), c) surfaces a typed event stream to the application, and d) manages transparent tool-call orchestration (retry, backoff, idempotency tokens, local optimistic responses).
3) Tool call extension: a small on-stream handshake to attach tool metadata (tool_id, semantic_version, invocation_token) and allow the SDK mediator to handle credentials exchange and local caching of tool responses for short-circuiting.

Design details
- Envelope: every stream frame may carry an optional header object: {schema_id, fragment_index, fragment_count, tool_meta?}. Implementation note: we will piggyback on the existing compact frame but require the header to be present only when a structured contract is specified.
- Incremental validation: use a streaming JSON-schema-ish validator (prototype uses Ajv streaming; server-side validation path will be in Rust runtime). Validator should accept partial tokens and mark the stream as synth-check-passed/failed. On failure, emit a structured diagnostic frame with recoverable vs non-recoverable flag.
- Reassembly logic: SDK mediator keeps fragments keyed by fragment index and ensures ordered emission. If fragments are missing for >Xms, mediator emits a 'partial-with-holes' marker and still exposes what it has to the app (configurable by strictness flag).
- Tool handshake flow (happy path): host stream -> server emits tool_meta with tool_id + invocation_token -> SDK forwards invocation_token to tool adapter (local) -> adapter can respond immediately (cached) or call remote tool and return result via mediator. Failure modes handled: tool-adapter error, token expired, network failure. Mediator applies policy (fail-open, fail-closed, fallthrough) configured per-route.

SDK ergonomics (developer UX)
- API shape: keep a single high-level object: RedwoodStream = new Redwood.Stream(request, {schema: 'project/x.y', toolAdapters: {...}})
  - events: on('partial'), on('schema-assert'), on('tool-request'), on('complete'), on('error')
  - convenience: RedwoodStream.intoTyped<T>(mapper) that returns a promise/async-iterator yielding typed frames for TypeScript consumers.
- Default behavior: strict=false (emit partials early), fallbacks=fail-open for interactive chat routes, fail-closed for financial-regulated routes. Project-level defaults can be overridden per-invocation.
- Smallfootprint: aim for <25KB minified for web SDK; native SDKs implement the same mediator logic but link to platform JSON-parser.

Observability and telemetry
- New event types to track: schema_validation_pass, schema_validation_fail, fragment_missing, tool_handshake_success, tool_handshake_fail, tool_adapter_cache_hit. Each event includes route, model, schema_id, customer_id, and latency buckets.
- Console UI: per-schema health dashboard (validation rate, average fragments per response, top failure reasons). Add a 'schema regressions' alert that ties to the Eval infra.

Backward compatibility and migration
- Schema offload is opt-in. Old clients continue to receive full streams without headers. Servers will only add schema headers when the invocation includes the schema parameter.
- Provide a compatibility shim: server can emit an optional 'compat_snapshot' frame containing the best-effort flat string concatenation for legacy clients (configurable TTL).

Safety and failure modes
- If validation fails and the schema has 'reject_on_failure' true, the runtime will emit an explicit end-of-stream with error code and no tool-call triggers executed. This prevents propogation of bad structured outputs to tools.
- If a tool adapter is untrusted, SDK mediator will only forward a hashed minimal token instead of full creds and request server-side orchestration (configurable).

Rollout plan (quarters)
- Q1 (experiment): internal SDK prototypes + two early-adopter customers; metric instrumentation scaffolding.
- Q2 (stabilize): hardened mediator, streaming-validator in Rust runtime, public SDK beta, gating on validation pass rates.
- Q3 (general availability): console integration, schema registry minor UI, default telemetry dashboards, and migration guides.

Open questions / risks (short list)
- How to support non-JSON structured outputs (markup, binary)? Proposal: schema layer is format-typed; for non-JSON we use a content-encoding header and a format plugin in SDKs.
- Cost of additional server-side validation—need perf microbenchmarks vs baseline to confirm <5% p99 tail increase.
- Handling cross-route tool semantics: some tools have side effects and cannot be re-played safely. Need per-tool idempotency metadata and server-side enforcement.

Action items (owners)
- Prototype SDK mediator (web + node): Evan Lee — prototype by 2026-01-31
- Streaming validator PoC in runtime: Liu Chen — PoC by 2026-02-15
- Console schema registry minimal UI: Priya Desai — initial mock by 2026-02-01
- Early-adopter outreach and onboarding doc: Sofia Martinez — outreach list by 2026-01-20

Appendix: notes from related threads
- Refer to GH PR: redwood-inference/sdk#487 for initial mediator shim and event types.
- Confluence sketch: /display/PRD/hosted-api-schema-first for research notes and kata traces.
- Slack thread: #hosted-api-schema where early ergonomics feedback is collected (selection pasted below).

Informal notes / brainstorm fragments
- "We should make the mediator re-emit a compact 'human preview' frame for debugging so mobile clients can show progressive text while the typed object is validated."
- "Tool adapters as local pluggable modules will let customers keep secrets client-side and only pass tokens — reduces regulatory friction for Private deployments."

This doc is intentionally a working draft. Please add comments inline, link PRs to GH: redwood-inference/sdk and tag eng-serving-runtime for perf estimates.
